claim: The investigation of the neural mechanisms underlying the generation of locomotion has unraveled considerable detail on how neural networks that produce the basic motor outputs for swimming, flying and walking of invertebrates and vertebrates are organized and operate.
source: The investigation of the neural mechanisms underlying the generation of locomotion has unraveled considerable detail on how those neural networks that produce the basic motor outputs for swimming, flying and walking of invertebrates and vertebrates are organized and operate (Grillner et al., 2008; Goulding, 2009; Lehmann, 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Grillner et al., 2008; Goulding, 2009; Lehmann, 2004)

claim: At the level of the locomotor organs, a basic motor output is the result of the activity of local central pattern generating networks (CPGs) and its adjustment through sensory feedback from the locomotor organs.
source: At the level of the locomotor organs, a basic motor output is the result of the activity of local central pattern generating networks (CPGs), and its adjustment through sensory feedback from the locomotor organs (Büschges and Gruhn, 2008; Pearson, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Büschges and Gruhn, 2008; Pearson, 2008)

claim: Load is particularly important for the control of the step cycle.
source: Particularly important for the control of the step cycle in this context is load (Schmitz and Stein, 2000; Duysens et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Schmitz and Stein, 2000; Duysens et al., 2000)

claim: Evidence suggests that descending signals from brain centers such as reticulospinal neurons in the vertebrate hind brain/basal ganglia or the head ganglia of arthropods contribute to both the basic drive and its modulation.
source: Evidence suggests that descending signals from brain centers such as reticulospinal neurons in the vertebrate hind brain/basal ganglia (Stephenson-Jones et al., 2011) or the head ganglia of arthropods with the putative arthropod basal ganglia homolog (Strausfeld and Hirth, 2013), the central complex in the cerebral ganglion (Strauss and Heisenberg, 1993; Guo and Ritzmann, 2013; Bidaye et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2015) contribute to both the basic drive and its modulation (Brocard et al., 2010; Shik et al., 1969; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: How descending signals influence the motor activity at the level of the local neural networks that control the locomotor organs is only beginning to be understood, in particular for walking.
source: How these descending signals influence the motor activity at the level of the local neural networks that control the locomotor organs, however, is only beginning to be understood, in particular for walking, the most ubiquitous form of locomotion in terrestrial animals (Ridgel et al., 2007; Dyson et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Ridgel et al., 2007; Dyson et al., 2014; Martin et al., 2015)

claim: All walking animals need to change the kinematics of each leg substantially when changing course in order to separate the activity between the leg and body segments and produce the appropriate locomotor movements on the two body sides.
source: When changing course, all walking animals need to change the kinematics of each leg substantially in order to separate the activity between the leg and body segments and produce the appropriate locomotor movements on the two body sides (Jander, 1985; Gruhn et al., 2009; Rivera et al., 2006; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Mu and Ritzmann, 2005; Jindrich and Full, 1999; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Musienko et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: In a six-legged curve walking insect, outside legs push the animal, while inside legs pull the animal into the direction of the curve.
source: In a six-legged curve walking insect, for example, outside legs push the animal, while inside legs pull the animal into the direction of the curve (Jindrich and Full, 1999; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Gruhn et al., 2009), sometimes even reversing the stepping direction in single inside legs (Gruhn et al., 2009; Cruse et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Jindrich and Full, 1999; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Gruhn et al., 2009)

claim: Inside legs sometimes reverse the stepping direction in single legs during curve walking.
source: In a six-legged curve walking insect, for example, outside legs push the animal, while inside legs pull the animal into the direction of the curve (Jindrich and Full, 1999; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Gruhn et al., 2009), sometimes even reversing the stepping direction in single inside legs (Gruhn et al., 2009; Cruse et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Gruhn et al., 2009; Cruse et al., 2009)

claim: Little insight exists into how the nervous system generates motor flexibility during turning.
source: Currently, little insight exists, into how the nervous system generates such motor flexibility (Guo and Ritzmann, 2013; Huang et al., 2013; Hellekes et al., 2012; Ridgel et al., 2007; Fagerstedt et al., 2001; McClellan, 1984; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Sensory input from vestibular/antennal or optical areas is processed in the brains of vertebrates and insects and transformed into descending neuronal signals that induce changes in the activity of the local networks which produce the ongoing motor patterns.
source: It seems clear that sensory input from vestibular/antennal or optical areas is processed in the brains of vertebrates and insects alike, and transformed into descending neuronal signals that induce changes in the activity of the local networks which produce the ongoing motor patterns (Guo and Ritzmann, 2013; Mu and Ritzmann, 2008a; Ridgel et al., 2007; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1993; Huang et al., 2013; Musienko et al., 2012; McClellan, 1984; Martin et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work

claim: The nature of changes that generate body-side-specific motor output during turning is still largely unknown.
source: The nature of these changes that generate body-side-specific motor output, however, is still largely unknown.
evidence: Statement about the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: The average period of front leg inside steps (0.83s) was significantly shorter than that of front leg outside steps (1.21s) in 11 out of 14 sequences.
source: Quantitative analysis of 14 inside and outside curve walking sequences from 10 intact animals showed that the period of front leg (FL) inside steps (Pin=0.83s; SD=0.21) between animals was significantly shorter than that of FL outside steps (Pout=1.21s; SD=0.37) in 11 out of 14 sequences (p<0.05).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data from 14 sequences from 10 animals with statistical significance p<0.05

claim: The average period of middle leg inside steps (0.76s) was significantly shorter than that of middle leg outside steps (1.13s).
source: Likewise, the average period of middle leg (ML) inside steps (Pin=0.76s; SD=0.15) was significantly shorter than that of ML outside steps (Pout=1.13s; SD=0.28) (p<0.01, Figure Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by quantitative analysis of experimental data with statistical significance p<0.01, shown in Figure 1a

claim: The stepping periods of the inside front legs and middle legs were not significantly different from one another.
source: Neither the stepping periods of the inside, nor those of the outside FLs and MLs were significantly different from one another (pin =0.43s, pout= 0.6s, Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1a

claim: The stepping periods of the outside front legs and middle legs were not significantly different from one another.
source: Neither the stepping periods of the inside, nor those of the outside FLs and MLs were significantly different from one another (pin =0.43s, pout= 0.6s, Figure 1a).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 1a

claim: The only clear difference in the average EMG activity between inside and outside legs was observed in the thorax-coxa-joint.
source: We also looked for changes in motor output at the level of the muscle activity between the inside and outside legs. The only clear difference in the average EMG activity was observed in the most proximal leg joint, the thorax-coxa-joint, through which movements of a leg along the body axis are controlled.
evidence: Based on analysis of EMG recordings from multiple muscles

claim: During inside stepping, the retractor coxae and protractor coxae muscles both served as either stance or swing muscles.
source: During inside stepping, the muscles retractor coxae and its antagonist, the protractor coxae, both served as either stance or swing muscles.
evidence: Based on EMG recordings during inside stepping

claim: The protractor activation during inside stepping often overlapped with that of the retractor, suggesting co-contraction.
source: Interestingly, the protractor activation in this case often also overlapped with that of the retractor, which suggests co-contraction and matches sideward steps observed during inside stepping.
evidence: Based on EMG recordings showing overlapping activation patterns

claim: Depressor activity on the outside was slightly prolonged.
source: In addition, depressor activity on the outside was slightly prolonged (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental data (not shown in manuscript)

claim: The findings corroborate the relative independence of the CPGs for each joint and between hemiganglia.
source: Altogether, these findings corroborate the relative independence of the CPGs for each joint, and between hemiganglia that has been long known (Büschges et al., 1995; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005).
evidence: Inference from experimental findings supported by citations to prior work (Büschges et al., 1995; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005)

claim: During outside stepping sequences, load stimuli either initiated or enhanced retractor activity.
source: During outside stepping sequences, load stimuli either initiated or enhanced retractor activity (Figure 2; 359 stimuli during outside walking in 13 animals).
evidence: Based on 359 load stimuli during outside walking in 13 animals, shown in Figure 2

claim: The timing of the load stimuli with respect to the front leg steps was distributed uniformly around FL stepping activity during outside stepping.
source: The timing of the load stimuli with respect to the front leg steps was distributed uniformly around FL stepping activity (Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of timing data shown in Figure 2c and Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Processing of loading signals on the outside of curve walking animals is similar to straight stepping and ensures leg retraction throughout stance.
source: Processing of loading signals on the outside of curve walking animals is thus similar to straight stepping and ensures leg retraction throughout stance (Akay et al., 2007; Borgmann et al., 2009).
evidence: Inference from experimental data supported by citations to prior work (Akay et al., 2007; Borgmann et al., 2009)

claim: On the inside, the response to a loading stimulus was markedly different from the outside.
source: On the inside, however, the response to a loading stimulus was markedly different.
evidence: Based on comparison of experimental data from inside and outside stepping

claim: Upon start of FL inside stepping, the mesothoracic protractor MNs showed an increase in activity.
source: Upon start of FL inside stepping, the mesothoracic protractor MNs showed an increase in activity.
evidence: Based on motor neuron recordings during inside stepping

claim: No stereotypical activation of retractor activity was observed upon load stimuli during inside stepping.
source: In contrast to the standing animal, however, no stereotypical activation of retractor activity was observed upon load stimuli (n=617).
evidence: Based on 617 load stimuli during inside stepping

claim: Load stimuli either started or terminated retractor activity, and vice versa, protractor activity during inside stepping.
source: Instead, load stimuli either started or terminated retractor, and vice versa, protractor activity.
evidence: Based on analysis of motor neuron responses to load stimuli during inside stepping

claim: Activation of the retractor MNs in variable strength compared to control upon load stimuli was observed in all 13 animals during inside stepping.
source: Activation of the retractor MNs in variable strength compared to control upon load stimuli was observed in all 13 animals (16–100% of the stimuli/animal), termination of retractor, and activation of protractor MNs was observed in 54% of the cases (7 out of 13 animals, 2–25% of the stimuli).
evidence: Based on experimental data from all 13 animals tested

claim: Termination of retractor and activation of protractor MNs was observed in 54% of the cases (7 out of 13 animals, 2–25% of the stimuli) during inside stepping.
source: Activation of the retractor MNs in variable strength compared to control upon load stimuli was observed in all 13 animals (16–100% of the stimuli/animal), termination of retractor, and activation of protractor MNs was observed in 54% of the cases (7 out of 13 animals, 2–25% of the stimuli).
evidence: Based on experimental data from 7 out of 13 animals

claim: In 10 out of 13 animals, and on average upon 18.8% of the stimuli, load stimuli did neither elicit retractor nor protractor activation during inside stepping.
source: In addition, in 10 out of 13 animals, and on average upon 18.8% of the stimuli (SD=15.2), load stimuli did neither elicit retractor nor protractor activation.
evidence: Based on experimental data from 10 out of 13 animals

claim: Timing of the load stimuli with respect to the front leg steps was distributed uniformly throughout the FL step cycle during inside stepping.
source: Timing of the load stimuli with respect to the front leg steps was distributed uniformly throughout the FL step cycle.
evidence: Based on analysis of timing data during inside stepping

claim: The strength of the retractor activation was not dependent on the timing of the CS stimulus during the FL step cycle.
source: We also tested whether the strength of the retractor activation was dependent on the timing of the CS stimulus during the FL step cycle. This was not the case, as shown in the plot in Figure 3c for the example animal shown in Figure 3a, nor for all other animals (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Based on analysis shown in Figure 3c and Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for all animals

claim: No phase preference was found for the activation of protractor activity during FL step cycle.
source: We equally tested whether either activation of the protractor motor activity or the lack of a response occurred during a preferred phase of the step cycle. No phase preference was found for the activation of protractor activity during FL step cycle (Figure 3d).
evidence: Based on phase analysis shown in Figure 3d

claim: A significantly increased likelihood for failure to elicit a response to a CS stimulus was found at 0.89 of the FL step cycle (p=0.028).
source: However, we found a significantly increased likelihood for failure to elicit a response to a CS stimulus at 0.89 of the FL step cycle (p=0.028) although this phenomenon could occur during all phases of the FL step cycle (Figure 3e).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis with p=0.028, shown in Figure 3e

claim: The results show side-specificity in the processing of local load signals during inside curve walking, modified from that during forward and outward stepping, such that the stereotypical influence of load feedback is no longer present.
source: In summary, these results clearly show side-specificity in the processing of local load signals during inside curve walking, modified from that during forward and outward stepping, such that the stereotypical influence of load feedback is no longer present.
evidence: Summary inference from the experimental data on load feedback processing

claim: When the FL performed inside steps, protractor activity in the mesothorax was increased over retractor activity in all animals (N=17).
source: When the FL performed inside steps, protractor activity in the mesothorax was increased over retractor activity in all animals (N=17), and alternating activity between the two MN pools was observed (Figure 4a).
evidence: Based on motor neuron recordings from all 17 animals, shown in Figure 4a

claim: Alternating activity between the protractor and retractor MN pools was observed during inside stepping.
source: When the FL performed inside steps, protractor activity in the mesothorax was increased over retractor activity in all animals (N=17), and alternating activity between the two MN pools was observed (Figure 4a).
evidence: Based on motor neuron recordings shown in Figure 4a

claim: The rhythmic activity of the mesothoracic coxal motoneurons was tightly correlated and largely in phase with the steps of the ipsilateral FL during inside stepping.
source: The rhythmic activity of the mesothoracic coxal motoneurons was tightly correlated and largely in phase with the steps of the ipsilateral FL, as previously described for straight walking of the FL on a treadmill (Borgmann et al., 2007) (Figure 4bi–ii).
evidence: Based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 4bi–ii, supported by citation to prior work (Borgmann et al., 2007)

claim: Protractor activity was strongest at about 270° of the step cycle in the FL in about 60% of the experiments (N=17) during inside stepping.
source: Protractor activity was strongest at about 270° of the step cycle in the FL in about 60% of the experiments (N=17), retractor activity at about 90° in 86% of the experiments (N=14) (Figure 4ci–ii).
evidence: Based on phase analysis from 17 experiments, shown in Figure 4ci–ii

claim: Retractor activity was strongest at about 90° of the step cycle in 86% of the experiments (N=14) during inside stepping.
source: Protractor activity was strongest at about 270° of the step cycle in the FL in about 60% of the experiments (N=17), retractor activity at about 90° in 86% of the experiments (N=14) (Figure 4ci–ii).
evidence: Based on phase analysis from 14 experiments, shown in Figure 4ci–ii

claim: During very few inside turning sequences protractor activity became almost tonic, while retractor activity was almost absent.
source: During very few inside turning sequences protractor activity became almost tonic, while retractor activity was almost absent.
evidence: Based on observations from a small subset of inside turning sequences

claim: During outside turns of the ipsilateral FL, protractor activity was strongly reduced compared to retractor activity.
source: In contrast, during outside turns of the ipsilateral FL, protractor activity was strongly reduced compared to retractor activity, and the activity of both motor neuron pools was no longer alternating, but generally tonic (Npro=17, Nret=15; Figure 4d).
evidence: Based on motor neuron recordings from 17 animals (protractor) and 15 animals (retractor), shown in Figure 4d

claim: The activity of both motor neuron pools was no longer alternating, but generally tonic during outside turns.
source: In contrast, during outside turns of the ipsilateral FL, protractor activity was strongly reduced compared to retractor activity, and the activity of both motor neuron pools was no longer alternating, but generally tonic (Npro=17, Nret=15; Figure 4d).
evidence: Based on motor neuron recordings from 17 animals (protractor) and 15 animals (retractor), shown in Figure 4d

claim: No significant phase coupling to the FL steps was present in the majority of cases during outside turns, in about 76% of the animals for the protractor, and in 80% of the animals for the retractor.
source: Consequently, no significant phase coupling to the FL steps was present in the majority of cases, that is in about 76% of the animals for the protractor, and in 80% of the animals for the retractor (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: Based on phase coupling analysis shown in Figure 4e–f

claim: Coxal motoneuron activity on the inside of the curve walking animal was rhythmic and alternating, coupled to front leg stepping.
source: In summary, coxal motoneuron activity on the inside of the curve walking animal was rhythmic and alternating, coupled to front leg stepping, while motoneuron activity on the outside was tonic and mostly limited to the retractor motoneurons.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on motoneuron activity patterns

claim: Motoneuron activity on the outside was tonic and mostly limited to the retractor motoneurons.
source: In summary, coxal motoneuron activity on the inside of the curve walking animal was rhythmic and alternating, coupled to front leg stepping, while motoneuron activity on the outside was tonic and mostly limited to the retractor motoneurons.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on motoneuron activity patterns

claim: Pilocarpine elicited slow, alternating motor activity in the standing animal.
source: We therefore isolated the mesothoracic ganglion in a split-bath preparation, and, after recording mesothoracic pro- and retractor activity in control conditions (Figure 5ai, 6ai), activated the local CPGs in the mesothoracic ganglion pharmacologically through superfusion with the muscarinic agonist pilocarpine (Büschges, 1995;Borgmann et al., 2009). This elicited slow, alternating motor activity in the standing animal (Figure 5aii, 6aii, aiii).
evidence: Based on experimental observations with pilocarpine application, shown in Figures 5aii, 6aii, aiii, supported by citations to prior work (Büschges, 1995;Borgmann et al., 2009)

claim: During subsequent inside steps of the ipsilateral FL, protractor activity increased, and the pilocarpine-induced rhythm sped up significantly in all experiments from an average 0.27Hz to 1.16 Hz (N=11, p<0.001).
source: During subsequent inside steps of the ipsilateral FL, protractor activity increased, and the pilocarpine-induced rhythm sped up significantly in all experiments from an average 0.27Hz (SD=0.1) to 1.16 Hz (SD=0.36; N=11, p<0.001; Figure 5b).
evidence: Based on experimental data from 11 animals with statistical significance p<0.001, shown in Figure 5b

claim: In about two thirds of the cases (62.5%; N=8) the frequency of the rhythmic mesothoracic MN activity was not significantly different from that of the stepping FL during inside stepping with pilocarpine.
source: In about two thirds of the cases (62.5%; N=8) the frequency of the rhythmic mesothoracic MN activity was not significantly different from that of the stepping FL.
evidence: Based on frequency analysis from 8 animals

claim: Phase-coupling of mesothoracic MN activity to FL stepping was present during inside stepping with pilocarpine, with protractor activity peaking around 270°, and retractor activity around 90° of the step cycle.
source: Likewise, phase-coupling of mesothoracic MN activity to FL stepping was present, with protractor activity peaking around 270°, and retractor activity around 90° of the step cycle (Figure 5c,d).
evidence: Based on phase analysis shown in Figure 5c,d

claim: During outside turns of the FL with pilocarpine, retractor activity in the mesothoracic segment was strongly increased.
source: In contrast, during outside turns of the FL, similar to the control condition without pilocarpine, retractor activity in the mesothoracic segment was strongly increased (Figure 6ai).
evidence: Based on motor neuron recordings shown in Figure 6ai

claim: No increase in mean frequency of the protractor/retractor MN activity was observed during outside turns with pilocarpine (N=8).
source: No increase in mean frequency of the protractor/retractor MN activity was observed (N=8; Fctrl=0.27, SD= 0.12, Fout=0.33, SD= 0.16), and the frequency was always significantly lower than that of the stepping FL (N=5; Figure 6b).
evidence: Based on frequency analysis from 8 animals, shown in Figure 6b

claim: The frequency of protractor/retractor MN activity was always significantly lower than that of the stepping FL during outside turns with pilocarpine (N=5).
source: No increase in mean frequency of the protractor/retractor MN activity was observed (N=8; Fctrl=0.27, SD= 0.12, Fout=0.33, SD= 0.16), and the frequency was always significantly lower than that of the stepping FL (N=5; Figure 6b).
evidence: Based on frequency comparison from 5 animals, shown in Figure 6b

claim: In individual walking sequences during outside turns with pilocarpine, the frequency of coxal motoneuron activity appeared to be locked in retractor phase.
source: In individual walking sequences, the frequency of coxal motoneuron activity even appeared to be locked in retractor phase (Figure 6aii and aiii).
evidence: Based on observations shown in Figure 6aii and aiii

claim: No systematic phase coupling to the outside stepping FL was present during outside turns with pilocarpine.
source: No systematic phase coupling to the outside stepping FL was present, again similar to controls (Figure 6c,d).
evidence: Based on phase analysis shown in Figure 6c,d

claim: Side-specific changes in mesothoracic motor activity occur during turning that result from local changes in CPG activity.
source: In summary, our results thus show that side-specific changes in mesothoracic motor activity occur during turning that result from local changes in CPG activity.
evidence: Summary inference from experimental results on CPG activity

claim: Changes in local motor activity appear to be influenced by FL stepping on the inside but not the outside.
source: These changes in local motor activity appear to be influenced by FL stepping on the inside but not the outside.
evidence: Inference from experimental observations of motor activity patterns

claim: Lesioning the connective between the pro- and mesothoracic ganglia ipsilateral to the recording site abolished all of the turning-related modifications of MN activity during curve stepping (N=4).
source: To test whether these side-specific modifications of the mesothoracic motor output were based either on descending unilateral drive, through the corresponding connective, or bilateral drive through both connectives, we lesioned the connective between the pro- and mesothoracic ganglia ipsilateral to the recording site. This lesion abolished all of the above described modifications of MN activity during curve stepping (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, N=4), incl. the influence on the activity of the segmental CPGs in the split-bath configuration (N=2), while the contralateral activity on the intact side remained unaffected.
evidence: Based on lesion experiments in 4 animals, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: Lesioning the ipsilateral connective abolished the influence on the activity of the segmental CPGs in the split-bath configuration (N=2).
source: To test whether these side-specific modifications of the mesothoracic motor output were based either on descending unilateral drive, through the corresponding connective, or bilateral drive through both connectives, we lesioned the connective between the pro- and mesothoracic ganglia ipsilateral to the recording site. This lesion abolished all of the above described modifications of MN activity during curve stepping (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, N=4), incl. the influence on the activity of the segmental CPGs in the split-bath configuration (N=2), while the contralateral activity on the intact side remained unaffected.
evidence: Based on lesion experiments in 2 animals in split-bath configuration

claim: The contralateral activity on the intact side remained unaffected after lesioning the ipsilateral connective.
source: To test whether these side-specific modifications of the mesothoracic motor output were based either on descending unilateral drive, through the corresponding connective, or bilateral drive through both connectives, we lesioned the connective between the pro- and mesothoracic ganglia ipsilateral to the recording site. This lesion abolished all of the above described modifications of MN activity during curve stepping (Figure 5—figure supplement 1, N=4), incl. the influence on the activity of the segmental CPGs in the split-bath configuration (N=2), while the contralateral activity on the intact side remained unaffected.
evidence: Based on observations from lesion experiments

claim: The modifications in mesothoracic motor activity observed during FL curve stepping are the result of unilateral information flow through the ipsilateral connectives.
source: These findings demonstrate that the modifications in mesothoracic motor activity observed during FL curve stepping are the result of unilateral information flow through the ipsilateral connectives.
evidence: Inference from lesion experiments showing that ipsilateral lesions abolish modifications

claim: Animals walking on a surface with reduced mechanical coupling generate higher stepping frequencies in inside compared to outside legs.
source: We have shown that animals walking on a surface with reduced mechanical coupling generate higher stepping frequencies in inside compared to outside legs.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on stepping frequencies

claim: Protractor and retractor coxae muscles show major differences in activation during inside and outside stepping conditions.
source: Protractor and retractor coxae muscles show major differences in activation during both conditions.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on muscle activation patterns

claim: Processing of local load feedback is modified in a task-specific manner depending on the function of the leg as inside or outside leg.
source: Depending on the function of the leg as inside or outside leg, processing of local load feedback and the activity of the segmental CPG for the coxal motoneurons of the middle legs (ML) are modified in a task-specific manner.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on load feedback processing

claim: The activity of the segmental CPG for the coxal motoneurons of the middle legs is modified in a task-specific manner depending on the function of the leg as inside or outside leg.
source: Depending on the function of the leg as inside or outside leg, processing of local load feedback and the activity of the segmental CPG for the coxal motoneurons of the middle legs (ML) are modified in a task-specific manner.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings on CPG activity

claim: Body-side-specific changes participate in altering leg kinematics during optomotor-induced turning.
source: We conclude that these body-side-specific changes participate in altering leg kinematics during optomotor-induced turning.
evidence: Conclusion drawn from experimental findings

claim: Previous studies on curve walking reported varying degrees of decoupling and asymmetry between the limbs on the inside and outside of a curve.
source: Previous studies on curve walking reported varying degrees of decoupling and asymmetry between the limbs on the inside and outside of a curve (cat: (Musienko et al., 2012); turtle: (Rivera et al., 2006), stick insect: (Jander, 1985; Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Gruhn et al., 2009); cockroach: (Jindrich and Full, 1999; Mu and Ritzmann, 2005); crayfish: (Cruse and Saavedra, 1996); Drosophila: (Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990)).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior work across different species

claim: The success of the turning motor behavior can be deduced from changes in the stride length or from the sideward or backward steps or strokes of the inside leg.
source: The success of the turning motor behavior can either be deduced from changes in the stride length (Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990) or from the sideward or backward steps or strokes of the inside leg (Gruhn et al., 2009; Strauss and Heisenberg, 1990; Mu and Ritzmann, 2005; Rivera et al., 2006; Szczecinski et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: In the stick insect, the ML movement on the inside is characterized by a flexion around the femur-tibia joint, reduced angle of movement in the thorax-coxa joint, and the occurrence of forward, sideward and backward steps in immediate succession.
source: In the stick insect, the ML movement on the inside is characterized by a flexion around the femur-tibia joint, reduced angle of movement in the thorax-coxa joint, and the occurrence of forward, sideward and backward steps in immediate succession.
evidence: Description of kinematic characteristics in stick insect

claim: Outside MLs only show an increased front to back angle of movement, and reduced flexion in the femur tibia joint both under conditions of turning on normal substrate and during turns on the slippery surface.
source: In contrast, outside MLs only show an increased front to back angle of movement, and reduced flexion in the femur tibia joint both under conditions of turning on normal substrate and during turns on the slippery surface (Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Gruhn et al., 2009- , 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Gruhn et al., 2009- , 2011)

claim: Most studies on turning of arthropods have been performed on air cushioned balls, and reported a decrease in stepping frequency of the inside compared to the outside legs.
source: Most studies on turning of arthropods have been performed on air cushioned balls, and also reported a decrease in stepping frequency of the inside compared to the outside legs (Zolotov et al., 1975; Jander, 1985), sometimes no change in frequencies (Cruse and Saavedra, 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Zolotov et al., 1975; Jander, 1985; Cruse and Saavedra, 1996)

claim: All of the studies on air cushioned balls investigated curve walking while the individual legs of the animals were mechanically coupled through the ground, and could not express their inherent cycle period.
source: However, all of the studies cited above investigated curve walking while the individual legs of the animals were mechanically coupled through the ground, and could not express their inherent cycle period.
evidence: Inference about the conditions in prior studies

claim: A plausible explanation for the difference between prior findings and the current study is that curve walking was studied on a slippery surface.
source: A plausible explanation for the difference to our findings and similar ones in the cockroach (Mu and Ritzmann, 2005) is that we studied curve walking on a slippery surface.
evidence: Inference about the reason for differences in findings, supported by citation (Mu and Ritzmann, 2005)

claim: During walking above greased plates, the mechanical coupling between the legs, and passive influences caused by ground contact are reduced or even abolished.
source: During walking above greased plates, the mechanical coupling between the legs, and passive influences caused by ground contact are reduced or even abolished.
evidence: Inference about the effects of the experimental setup

claim: Stepping is not affected by passive displacement through the movements of the other legs on the ground via the mechanical coupling during walking on slippery surface.
source: In addition, stepping is not affected by passive displacement through the movements of the other legs on the ground via the mechanical coupling.
evidence: Inference about the effects of the experimental setup

claim: The resulting sensory feedback is altered from walking on normal ground during walking on slippery surface.
source: Hence, the resulting sensory feedback is altered from walking on normal ground.
evidence: Inference about the effects of the experimental setup

claim: Turning kinematics between slippery surface and air-cushioned ball are remarkably similar for both cockroach and stick insect.

source: Similarly, feedback from ML campaniform sensilla (CS) of stick insects, elicited by a load-mimicking stimulus in the horizontal plane, like that applied in our experiments, was shown to trigger a switch from ML protractor to retractor activity during forward, and in the opposite direction during backward stepping of the FL on a treadwheel (Akay et al., 2007).

evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Akay et al., 2007)

claim: All these changes in sensory processing could be depending on descending commands from the brain.
source: All these changes in sensory processing could be depending on descending commands from the brain, as lesioning the connective anterior to the prothoracic ganglion (Mu and Ritzmann, 2008b) and stimulation of turn-inducing central complex (CX) neurons have been shown to alter similar reflexes elicited by stimulation of the chordotonal organ in cockroach (Martin et al., 2015).

claim: Processing of a loading stimulus on the outside is similar to that during forward stepping, leading to retractor activation.

evidence: Inference from experimental results supported by citations to prior work (Dürr and Ebeling, 2005; Gruhn et al., 2009; Cruse et al., 2009)

source: A context-dependent influence of load feedback as part of a unilateral mechanism to generate behavioral adaptivity had been shown (Akay et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Akay et al., 2007)

claim: Graded input from yet unknown origin anterior to the mesothoracic ganglion during optomotor induced curve walking of the front legs locally modifies strength and sign of load stimulus-dependent influence.
source: From our results, it seems clear that graded input from yet unknown origin anterior to the mesothoracic ganglion during optomotor induced curve walking of the front legs locally modifies strength and sign of this load stimulus-dependent influence.

source: Alternatively, the weighing of parallel pathways from the load sensors, the CS, to the premotor interneurons could be shifted and thereby either promote retractor or protractor activation, as previously shown for gain control of reflexes (Driesang and Büschges, 1996) and recently implemented in a simulation model for cockroach turning (Szczecinski et al., 2014).

claim: The motor output in the deafferented mesothoracic motor control system is modified in a side-specific manner during curve walking of the FLs.
source: In addition, the motor output in the deafferented mesothoracic motor control system is also modified in a side-specific manner during curve walking of the FLs: first, there is pronounced alternating activity between pro- and retractor MNs on the inside, and tonic activity on the outside. Second, there is a strong bias towards protractor activation on the inside, and towards retractor activation on the outside.
evidence: Summary of experimental findings

claim: There is pronounced alternating activity between pro- and retractor MNs on the inside, and tonic activity on the outside during curve walking in the deafferented preparation.
source: In addition, the motor output in the deafferented mesothoracic motor control system is also modified in a side-specific manner during curve walking of the FLs: first, there is pronounced alternating activity between pro- and retractor MNs on the inside, and tonic activity on the outside.

source: Up to now, there are only two animal neural networks for which there exists a well founded idea on how turning is realized on the local level. The first are the networks that generate swimming in lamprey (Grillner et al., 2008), and the other are the networks that generate flight in locust (Rowell, 1993).

claim: In the locust, asymmetries in wing beat amplitude, phase shifts of wing beat between the sides, bending the abdomen and ruddering with the hind legs, all form part of steering maneuvers.

source: Especially, if the pronation angle in both wings on one side changes, turns are induced as a result of differences in lift and thrust between the two body sides (Wolf, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Wolf, 1990)

claim: These asymmetries in locust are created by activation of thoracic interneurons that receive input from descending interneurons about changes in body orientation.
source: These asymmetries are created by activation of thoracic interneurons that receive input from descending interneurons about changes in body orientation. This appears to directly affect MN output on one side of the body (Reichert, 1989; Rowell, 1993).

claim: In contrast to lamprey and the stick insect, in the locust, local CPG activity is unaffected by descending input during turning.

evidence: Supported by citation to prior work (Rowell, 1993)

source: In the curve walking stick insect, it is quite conceivable that a unilateral mechanism not completely unlike that in curve swimming lamprey is at work, as severing one of the two connectives between pro- and mesothoracic ganglion only prevented turning-related changes in motor activity on the lesioned side and not on the other.

source: The existence of a descending drive from anterior to the mesothoracic ganglion to the pattern generating networks of the mesothoracic joints was shown previously in physiological experiments (Westmark et al., 2009; Borgmann et al., 2007), and successfully implemented in models for the stick insect (Knops et al., 2013; Toth et al., 2012) and also for cockroach walking and turning (Szczecinski et al. 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (Westmark et al., 2009; Borgmann et al., 2007; Knops et al., 2013; Toth et al., 2012; Szczecinski et al. 2014)
